title: A Core Component
mood: Lesley brings home a piece of an Ender, whole. In Chang’e’s hands it starts to glow.

hero.alt: Lesley in the bright lab, her long gold hair with its red streak falling over her left eye, looks straight ahead with her lips just parted.

segs.t: Lesley was crossing the lab when Chang’e’s father lifted a core out of the raid crate with tongs.
It was black and split through, like a coal gone out.
“Slag,” said Chang’e’s mother, without looking up. “Again.”
He dropped it in the bin. The bin was nearly full. On her stool at the bench end, Chang’e looked at it and said nothing.
Lesley had watched cores die for years from the station wall.
They burn from the middle,
she thought.
The comm at her collar clicked twice, and its small green light blinked. Both the base and the Shield could reach her on it. Tonight the Shield was calling her out again.
An hour later she lay on a signal tower over the old rail yard at the city’s edge. Three Enders walked in among the rusted wagons.
A squad had gone to ground behind the nearest wagon. One Ender bent over it, reaching down.
Lesley stood up on the tower, where it could see her instead.
The Ender left the wagon and came for her.
It reached for the tower. Her sight sat on the middle of its chest, where years on the wall had put it.
Then she saw the bin again, and Chang’e on her stool, saying nothing.
A round in the middle would kill it and burn the core black. A round at the edge might only crack the core, and leave the Ender alive at arm’s length. She had never seen anyone try it.
The bolt Chang’e had filed twice was home. There would be time for one round.
She moved the sight off the middle, to where the edge would be.
The arm swung. The chest split open, and the core blazed so close she felt its heat. On her left side, the eye drew its rim in one thin teal line.
She fired.
A crack ran across the glow. The blow hit the tower, and the steel jumped under her. She held on with one hand.
The Ender went down among the wagons.
Most of its core burned out. One piece split away at the crack, before the burn reached it. It lay in the cinders, whole: a core component, a piece from deep inside the machine.
The squad’s sergeant stared at it. “They always burn,” he said.
Nobody had thought it could be done.
Lesley picked it up in her glove. It was dull. She carried it back in her fist.
Past midnight she set it on the Doctors’ bench.
Chang’e’s father turned it in his tongs under the lamp.
“Whole,” said Chang’e’s mother. She had put down her pen.
Chang’e was already off her stool, reaching for it.
“Gloves,” said her mother.
Chang’e stopped, hand out. “Sis. Did you break it like that on purpose?”
“I shot the edge,” said Lesley. “I didn’t know a piece would come off whole.”
Then she walked her round.
For eleven days the piece told Chang’e’s parents nothing.
They ran current through it and heated it. The needles lay flat. Her father lifted it only with tongs, her mother only in gloves. That was the lab’s rule for anything off an Ender.
The lab’s gloves came up to Chang’e’s elbows.
Inefficient.
On the twelfth evening the Shield called Sis out again.
Chang’e took the gloves off to rewire a meter. She needed the piece’s clamp. Nobody was looking, so she held the piece in both hands.
“She’s back at nine,” she told Mr. Bunny. “She said nine. Sis does what she says.”
Mr. Bunny’s screen went to two round eyes.
Chang’e looked down. A light had woken inside the piece. It was small and pale, and it trembled.
She did not breathe. The light stayed.
The clock over the door said nine. Then a quarter past.
She’s late,
thought Chang’e.
Sis is never late.
The light thinned. By half past it was a thread.
The gate bolt banged. Boots crossed the yard with the long, even stride Chang’e had followed down every corridor.
The light came up so fast she nearly dropped it.
She ran around to the front of her parents’ bench, where they could see, and held it up.
Her mother set down her mug. Her father took off his glasses.
“It listens to me!” said Chang’e.
Her mother looked from the light to Chang’e.
“A guess is not a claim,” she said gently. “Test it.”
Her father put his glasses back on.
So they tested it, with a meter and a notebook.
“Think of your Sis,” said her mother.
The needle climbed.
“Now think of nothing.”
Chang’e screwed up her face. The needle did not move.
“I can’t,” she said. “Sis keeps getting in.”
“Seven times eight.”
“Fifty-six.” The needle dropped, and the light went out.
Her father wrote that one down himself.
After two weeks, Chang’e pushed her glasses up her nose and read the notebook back.
“It doesn’t care what I know,” she said. “It cares what I believe.” She frowned at the page. “And only while I hold on.”
Two nights later, at supper, Chang’e stopped with her spoon in the soup.
If believing lights it,
she thought,
anyone can. A soldier could.
She slid off her chair. “When an idea comes to me, I go straight back to the lab.”
Her mother laughed.
“Sit,” said Lesley, from the fourth place.
Chang’e did not sit. “It needs a frame. The core in the chest, where an Ender keeps it. And a soldier inside, believing.”
Her father reached into his pocket and laid a folded napkin beside her bowl.
Thirty kilos. Twenty, if she has to run far.
Sis’s numbers, in her father’s hand.
“Dad,” said Chang’e. “You kept that.”
He picked up his spoon again.
They built the frame at the back of the lab, beside the test ring.

Her father bent steel tube into the shape of a person, a head taller than Sis. He bolted on the dead gray plates from the benches. He weighed every plate first. The napkin hung on a nail above the scale.
In the middle of the chest he set the piece in a cage of wire. The right hand stood open, palm out. Chang’e fitted a copper plate into the palm herself, for a hand to press.
If it worked, a soldier would wear it: the first suit anyone had ever built.
Her mother’s notes filled one notebook, then a second, in her quick hand. The first page said who it was for, the way all her projects began. She pinned it to the frame’s foot.
For whoever has to stand in front.
Her mother had put a fourth stool by the frame. At midnight Lesley’s round stopped at the lab door, as it always did. Then she came in and sat on it.
Chang’e pressed her palm to the copper plate and thought of Sis, sitting right there. The piece lit in its cage. It shook, then held, while her mother counted out loud.
At eleven it went out.
“Not yet,” said her mother, and wrote down eleven.
Lesley read the pinned page. She stayed for two more tests, though her round was waiting.
The officer who had posted Lesley to the base came out himself. He would not give these orders over the comm.

“You brought in a core piece whole,” he said. “That makes you the most valuable shot the Shield has. Headquarters calls it a miracle. You’re going on a mission. Top secret. You’ll learn where on the road.”
“How long?”
“As long as it takes. No radio. No letters. We think the Enders can hear our signals.”
“And the base?”
“Another soldier takes your gate.”
The piece had made her worth sending away. Lesley saw that, and set it aside. In the Shield she had never refused an order.
“Understood.”
At dawn the two Doctors walked her down to the gate. Chang’e’s father kept his hands in his pockets. Chang’e’s mother held hers out.
The first time Lesley stood at this gate, she had only looked at that hand. Now she took it.
“We’ll set your plate,” said Chang’e’s mother.
Chang’e’s father took one hand out of his pocket. He laid it on Lesley’s shoulder, once, and put it back.
Chang’e stood in front of her with Mr. Bunny at her shoulder. Her coat was buttoned wrong.
“It held for two hundred and six last night,” she said. “Mom says one more week, and it holds for good. She calls that the first light.”
“Good.”
“Be back for it.”
“I’ll be back.”
Chang’e took hold of her coat sleeve. “Promise.”
Lesley looked down at the small hand.
Her brother had held her sleeve like that every night, and every night she had promised. She had kept it. He had died anyway. She had not promised anyone anything since.
“I promise,” said Lesley.
Chang’e let go of the sleeve.
On the road outside the gate, she keyed the comm at her collar, for the base’s log.
“Switching to stealth mode.”
She switched it off. The small green light went out.
